About: Ohm's Law

Source

Model
V ∈ [0.1, 9.0] V, R ∈ [10, 1000] Ω, I = V/R shown in mA to 0.1 mA.
Concept
Ohm's law — the current through a resistor is set jointly by the voltage pushing it and the resistance opposing it: I = V/R.
Serves
Both proportionalities in one picture: I ∝ V at fixed R (linear) and I ∝ 1/R at fixed V (inverse), with the current arrows and electron drift scaling live and the battery stack growing one 1.5 V AA cell at a time.
Inquiry
Two knobs, one law — why does doubling V double I, while doubling R halves it?
Misconception
That a battery delivers a fixed current. It fixes the voltage; the current is negotiated with the resistance — the same battery drives a different current through a different R.

Guided Inquiry

1 · The circuit

A battery and a resistor form a single closed loop. The battery holds a fixed potential difference V across the resistor, whose resistance R opposes the flow. The current I is the rate at which charge crosses any point of the loop: the blue arrows give its conventional direction, and the electrons drift the other way.

2 · Predict: a stronger battery

The battery holds V = 4.5 V across R = 500 Ω and the current is 9.0 mA. The battery is swapped for a 9.0 V one, the same resistor staying in place. What is the new current?

3 · Voltage sweep

R stays at 500 Ω and V starts at 1.5 V. Raise the voltage to 3.0 V, then to 6.0 V, and compare each current reading with the one before it. Note how many 1.5 V cells the battery stack holds at each step.

4 · Predict: a larger resistor

The same 4.5 V battery now drives R = 250 Ω and the current is 18.0 mA. The resistor is replaced by a 500 Ω one. What is the new current?

5 · Resistance sweep

V stays at 4.5 V and R starts at 100 Ω. Raise the resistance to 200 Ω, then to 400 Ω, and compare the current at each step with the step before. Compare that pattern with the one the voltage sweep produced.

6 · What Ohm's law claims

R ≡ V/I defines the resistance of any component. Ohm's law is the further claim that R stays constant as V changes — true for a metal resistor at fixed temperature, as here, and false for a diode or a hot filament lamp, whose V–I graphs curve. Ohm's law is a property of the material, not a universal law.

01

At a glance

A battery and a resistor form one closed loop of wire, and charge flows around it. The sim lets you choose the battery's voltage and the resistor's resistance, then reads the current that results. This simple loop is the core of almost every circuit.

What you'll learn

  • How the current in a battery and resistor loop depends on the voltage and on the resistance.
  • How the voltage of a battery stack is built from 1.5 V cells.
  • How much heat the resistor receives, and what Ohm's law claims about a material.
One battery and one resistor in a single closed loop. The arrow marks the current I.

What's on screen

  • Battery stack (top wire): a row of copper cells, each labelled 1.5, with the total voltage V above it.
  • Resistor (bottom wire): a tan body with its resistance R below. It glows as it heats.
  • Current arrows and the badge current I: conventional current, in milliamperes.
  • Electrons (amber): they drift around the loop opposite to the arrows.
  • Readouts panel (sidebar): V, R and I as numbers.
See itPress Play at the opening values, V = 4.5 V and R = 500 Ω. Watch for: amber electrons circulating around the loop, against the direction of the blue arrows.

03

Current equals voltage divided by resistance

The battery holds a fixed potential difference V across the resistor, and the resistance R measures how strongly the resistor opposes the flow. The current I, the charge passing any point each second, is set by both:

I = V / R    (V = IR)
This is Ohm's law for a resistor: I in amperes, V in volts, R in ohms.

The sim reports milliamperes, so I(mA) = 1000 V/R. At the opening values, 4.5 V and 500 Ω, I = 4.5/500 = 0.0090 A, which is 9.0 mA. Neither the battery nor the resistor decides the current alone: both appear in the quotient. The same battery drives a different current through a different resistor.

See itPlay the opening values and read the current badge. Watch for: I = 9.0 mA in the Readouts panel, with 3 cells in the battery stack.
04

At fixed resistance the current is proportional to the voltage

Keep R at 500 Ω and change V. The quotient V/R changes in step, so doubling V doubles I and tripling V triples it. A graph of I against V is a straight line through the origin with slope 1/R, here 2.0 mA per volt. The battery stack shows the voltage as cells: a full cell for every 1.5 V, plus a part-cell for any remainder.

VCellsI at 500 Ω
1.5 V13.0 mA
3.0 V26.0 mA
4.5 V39.0 mA
6.0 V412.0 mA
9.0 V618.0 mA

Going from 4.5 V to 9.0 V adds three cells and doubles the current, from 9.0 to 18.0 mA. It does not quadruple it, because V appears to the first power in I = V/R.

See itRaise V to 9.0 V and keep R at 500 Ω. Watch for: the stack growing to 6 cells and I climbing to 18.0 mA.
05

At fixed voltage the current is inversely proportional to the resistance

Now keep V at 4.5 V and change R. Doubling R halves I, and halving R doubles it, because R sits in the denominator. The product I × R stays equal to V. For example, 45.0 mA × 100 Ω = 4.5 V, and 9.0 mA × 500 Ω = 4.5 V as well. A graph of I against R is a curve that falls steeply at first and then flattens, not a straight line.

RI at 4.5 VI × R
100 Ω45.0 mA4.5 V
200 Ω22.5 mA4.5 V
500 Ω9.0 mA4.5 V
1000 Ω4.5 mA4.5 V

So a battery does not deliver a fixed current. It fixes the voltage, and the current follows from whatever resistance is connected.

See itLower R to 250 Ω and keep V at 4.5 V. Watch for: I rising to 18.0 mA, twice its value at 500 Ω, with the same 3 cells.
06

The resistor turns electrical energy into heat

A charge q that crosses the potential difference V gives up energy qV. The charge passing each second is I, so the resistor receives energy at the rate

P = VI = I²R = V²/R
P in watts: the heating power of the resistor.

At 4.5 V and 500 Ω, P = 4.5 × 0.009 = 40.5 mW. Doubling V at the same R doubles I too, so P grows fourfold to 162 mW. The glow around the resistor tracks P, and is strongest at 9.0 V and 10 Ω, where I = 900 mA and P = 8.1 W. The current leaving the resistor equals the current entering. Charge is not used up, only its energy.

07

Where it matters

  • Ohm's law is not the definition of R. R ≡ V/I defines the resistance of any component. Ohm's law is the further claim that R stays constant as V changes. It holds for a metal at fixed temperature, as here. It fails for a diode and for a filament lamp, whose V–I graphs curve because R changes.
  • Choosing a resistor. To limit a 4.5 V supply to 15 mA, use R = 4.5/0.015 = 300 Ω. It then heats at 67.5 mW.
  • Short circuits. A very small R draws a very large current. 9.0 V across 10 Ω already drives 900 mA and 8.1 W, which is why fuses exist.
  • Cells in series. Each ideal 1.5 V cell adds its voltage, so n cells give 1.5n V. A real battery also has an internal resistance, which this sim leaves out.
08

Summary

In one line. The current in a battery and resistor loop is set by the voltage of the battery and the resistance of the resistor together.

Key points

  • I = V/R, so V = IR.
  • At fixed R, I ∝ V. At fixed V, I ∝ 1/R.
  • The resistor heats at P = VI = I²R = V²/R.
  • Ohm's law needs R to stay constant, which is true of a metal at fixed temperature.

Common mix-ups

  • "A battery always delivers the same current." It fixes the voltage. The current depends on the resistance connected.
  • "The arrow on the screen shows the exact current." Its size follows log I. The badge gives the exact value.
  • "Ohm's law holds for every component." It holds only where R stays constant as V changes.

Things to try on your own

  • Set V = 6.0 V and find the R that gives 20.0 mA, then check the readout.
  • Find two different pairs of V and R that give exactly 12.0 mA.
  • Turn off the electrons and keep the arrows, then do the reverse.
